title: How Computers Talk
explanation: Computer networking is how devices share information. Your phone, laptop, and smart TV all send data through networks. The internet is a massive network connecting billions of devices worldwide.
analogy: The internet is like a postal system. Each device has an address (IP address), you package data (packets), and routers deliver it to the destination.
example: You click a link. Your browser sends a request across the internet to a server. The server sends back the webpage. All in milliseconds.
why_it_matters: Almost everything is connected now. Understanding networking helps you understand how the modern world works.
checkpoint_question: What is the basic job of a computer network?
expected_answer: To transfer data between devices. This includes browsing the web, sending messages, streaming video, playing online games - all data moving between computers.
common_mistake: Thinking the internet and web are the same. The internet is the network infrastructure. The web (HTTP, websites) runs on top of it.
key_insight: The internet isn't owned by anyone. It's a network of networks - universities, companies, governments, and ISPs all connected together.

title: IP Addresses: Computer Locations
explanation: Every device on a network has an IP address - a unique number that identifies it. Like a house address, it tells the network where to send data. IPv4 looks like 192.168.1.1, IPv6 looks like longer hex numbers.
analogy: IP addresses are like street addresses. To send mail, you need to know the address. To send data, you need the IP address.
example: Your computer might be 192.168.1.100 on your home network. Google's servers have IPs like 142.250.80.46. Data goes between these addresses.
why_it_matters: IP addresses are fundamental to how the internet works. Every device communicating needs one.
checkpoint_question: Can two devices have the same IP address on the internet?
expected_answer: No, not on the public internet. Each public IP must be unique so data reaches the right destination. (On private networks like home WiFi, devices can have the same private IP as devices on other private networks.)
common_mistake: Thinking your IP address is permanent. It often changes, especially for home connections. This is called dynamic IP.
key_insight: IPv4 addresses are running out (only ~4 billion possible). IPv6 has enough addresses for every grain of sand on Earth.

title: DNS: The Internet's Phone Book
explanation: DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable names like 'google.com' into IP addresses like 142.250.80.46. Computers use IP addresses, but humans prefer names. DNS bridges this gap.
analogy: DNS is like a phone book. You look up a name (google.com), and it tells you the number (IP address) to call.
example: You type google.com. Your browser asks DNS: 'What's the IP for google.com?' DNS responds: '142.250.80.46'. Browser connects to that IP.
why_it_matters: Without DNS, you'd have to memorize IP addresses for every website. DNS makes the internet usable.
checkpoint_question: What happens if DNS is down?
expected_answer: You can't reach websites by name - google.com won't work. But if you know the IP address directly, you could still connect. DNS translates names to IPs, nothing more.
common_mistake: Thinking DNS is part of the website. It's a separate lookup service. The website and its DNS can be hosted in completely different places.
key_insight: DNS results are cached. Your computer remembers 'google.com = 142.250.80.46' for a while, so it doesn't ask DNS every time.

title: HTTP: Web Conversations
explanation: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is how web browsers and servers talk. The browser sends a request ('GET me this page'), the server sends a response (the page content). Every website uses HTTP (or its secure version, HTTPS).
analogy: Like ordering at a restaurant. You request (order), the kitchen responds (food). Simple request-response pattern.
example: Click a link: browser sends 'GET /news'. Server responds with HTML for the news page. Browser displays it.
why_it_matters: HTTP is the foundation of the web. Understanding it helps you understand how websites work and how to build them.
checkpoint_question: What's the difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
expected_answer: HTTPS is HTTP with encryption. The data is scrambled so only the browser and server can read it. This protects passwords, credit cards, and private data from being intercepted.
common_mistake: Entering passwords on HTTP (non-secure) sites. Anyone on the same network could read your password.
code:
# HTTP Request (what your browser sends)
GET /search?q=cats HTTP/1.1
Host: google.com

# HTTP Response (what the server returns)
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html

<html>...search results...</html>
key_insight: HTTP status codes tell you what happened: 200 = success, 404 = not found, 500 = server error. You've seen 404 pages!

title: Request Types: GET, POST, and More
explanation: HTTP has different request types (methods). GET retrieves data (load a page). POST sends data (submit a form). PUT updates data. DELETE removes data. The method tells the server what you want to do.
analogy: GET = 'give me this', POST = 'here's some data to process', PUT = 'update this', DELETE = 'remove this'. Different actions, same format.
example: Viewing a profile = GET. Submitting a login form = POST. Updating your email = PUT. Deleting a photo = DELETE.
why_it_matters: Understanding HTTP methods helps you understand how web apps work and how to build APIs.
checkpoint_question: Why use POST instead of GET for submitting a password?
expected_answer: GET puts data in the URL (visible, saved in history, logged). POST puts data in the request body (hidden, not saved in browser history). Never put passwords in URLs.
common_mistake: Using GET for sensitive data. Passwords in URLs can be cached, logged, and bookmarked - very insecure.
code:
# GET - retrieve data (no body)
GET /users/123 HTTP/1.1

# POST - send new data (has body)
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"username": "alice", "password": "secret"}

# PUT - update data
PUT /users/123 HTTP/1.1
{"email": "new@email.com"}
key_insight: RESTful APIs use these methods consistently: GET to read, POST to create, PUT to update, DELETE to remove. Clean and predictable.

title: APIs: Programs Talking to Programs
explanation: An API (Application Programming Interface) lets programs communicate. When an app shows weather, it asks a weather API for data. APIs return structured data (usually JSON) that programs can easily use.
analogy: APIs are like a restaurant menu for programs. The menu lists what you can order (available data/actions) and how to order it (request format).
example: Weather app: makes API call to weather service → gets JSON like {temp: 72, conditions: 'sunny'} → displays 'Sunny, 72°F'.
why_it_matters: Modern apps are built from APIs. Social login, payment processing, maps, weather - all APIs. Understanding them opens many possibilities.
checkpoint_question: Why do APIs return JSON instead of HTML?
expected_answer: HTML is for humans to read (visual layout). JSON is structured data that programs can easily parse and use. APIs serve programs, not people.
common_mistake: Scraping HTML instead of using APIs. APIs are designed to be used programmatically and are more reliable than parsing web pages.
code:
# Example API request
GET https://api.weather.com/current?city=Seattle

# Example JSON response
{
    "city": "Seattle",
    "temperature": 62,
    "unit": "F",
    "conditions": "Cloudy",
    "humidity": 75
}
key_insight: Public APIs often require an API key - a unique code that identifies your app and tracks your usage.

title: TCP: Reliable Delivery
explanation: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) guarantees data arrives completely and in order. It checks that all pieces arrived, requests re-sends of lost pieces, and assembles them correctly. Most internet traffic uses TCP.
analogy: TCP is like certified mail with tracking. You get confirmation of delivery, and if something is lost, it's re-sent until it arrives.
example: Downloading a file: TCP ensures every byte arrives. If a packet is lost, TCP detects this and requests it again. You get the complete file.
why_it_matters: TCP handles the complexity of reliable delivery so apps don't have to. Web, email, file transfers all rely on it.
checkpoint_question: What's the cost of TCP's reliability?
expected_answer: Speed and overhead. TCP needs to establish connections (handshake), track packets, wait for acknowledgments, and re-send lost data. This adds latency compared to just sending data and hoping.
common_mistake: Thinking all internet traffic uses TCP. Real-time video/gaming often uses UDP (faster, less reliable) instead.
key_insight: TCP starts with a 'three-way handshake' to establish connection: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. Only then does data flow.

title: UDP: Fast but Risky
explanation: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) just sends data without guarantees. No connection setup, no acknowledgment, no re-sends. Faster but packets can arrive out of order, duplicated, or not at all. The app must handle this.
analogy: UDP is like shouting across a room. Fast, but some words might not be heard. Good enough for some things, terrible for others.
example: Video call: if a packet is lost, don't wait - show the next frame. A blip is better than freezing while waiting for old data. That's why calls use UDP.
why_it_matters: Understanding when to use TCP vs UDP helps you understand why some apps behave differently (buffering vs real-time).
checkpoint_question: When would UDP be better than TCP?
expected_answer: Real-time applications where latency matters more than perfection: video calls, online gaming, live streaming. Old data is useless - skip it and continue with new data.
common_mistake: Using UDP for file transfers. A file with missing bytes is corrupted. Use TCP when completeness matters.
key_insight: Some apps build reliability on top of UDP to get the best of both: customizable reliability with lower latency than TCP.

title: HTTPS and Encryption
explanation: HTTPS encrypts the data between your browser and the website. Even if someone intercepts the traffic, they see scrambled nonsense. This protects passwords, credit cards, and private information.
analogy: HTTPS is like speaking in a secret code that only you and the website understand. Eavesdroppers hear gibberish.
example: Logging into your bank on public WiFi: with HTTPS, the hacker on the same network sees encrypted garbage. Without HTTPS, they'd see your password.
why_it_matters: HTTPS is essential for any sensitive data. Browsers now warn about non-HTTPS sites. Always look for the padlock icon.
checkpoint_question: Does HTTPS protect against all attacks?
expected_answer: No. HTTPS protects data in transit. It doesn't protect against malware on your computer, phishing (fake sites), or compromised servers. It's one layer of security, not complete protection.
common_mistake: Thinking a padlock means the site is trustworthy. The padlock only means the connection is encrypted. A scam site can also use HTTPS.
key_insight: HTTPS uses certificates to verify the site is who it claims to be. Certificate errors mean something might be wrong - don't ignore them!

title: Clients and Servers
explanation: A client asks for things. A server provides things. Your browser is a client - it requests web pages. Google's computer is a server - it sends web pages. Many clients connect to one server.
analogy: Clients are customers, servers are shopkeepers. Many customers visit one shop. The shop serves each customer's requests.
example: Netflix: millions of phone apps (clients) all request videos from Netflix's servers. Each client gets its own stream from the same servers.
why_it_matters: Client-server architecture is how most internet services work. Understanding it helps you understand web applications.
checkpoint_question: Can a computer be both a client and a server?
expected_answer: Yes! A web server might be a client when it requests data from a database server. It serves web pages to browsers while being a client to other services.
common_mistake: Thinking servers are special hardware. Any computer can be a server. It's about the role it plays, not the machine.
key_insight: Peer-to-peer (P2P) is different - computers act as both client and server simultaneously, sharing directly with each other (like BitTorrent).

title: Ports: Many Services, One IP
explanation: A port is a number that identifies which service on a computer should receive the data. One computer can run many services (web, email, database) - ports direct traffic to the right one. Like apartment numbers within a building.
analogy: IP address is the building address, port number is the apartment number. Mail goes to the building, but the apartment number tells which door.
example: Web servers use port 80 (HTTP) or 443 (HTTPS). When you visit google.com, you're really connecting to 142.250.80.46:443.
why_it_matters: Understanding ports helps you troubleshoot connection issues and understand how servers handle multiple services.
checkpoint_question: Why does your computer use a different port for each connection you make?
expected_answer: So responses can find their way back. If you have 10 browser tabs, each uses a different port. Responses include the port number so data goes to the right tab.
common_mistake: Thinking ports are physical things. They're just numbers in the data packets that identify which program should receive the data.
code:
# Common port numbers:
# 80   - HTTP (web)
# 443  - HTTPS (secure web)
# 22   - SSH (secure shell)
# 3306 - MySQL database
# 5432 - PostgreSQL database
# 6379 - Redis

# Full address: IP + port
# google.com:443
# localhost:3000 (local development server)
key_insight: Ports below 1024 are 'well-known ports' for standard services. Higher ports are used for custom applications and client connections.

title: Routers: Directing Traffic
explanation: Routers are like postal sorting facilities. They receive packets and decide where to send them next, based on the destination IP address. Data hops through many routers between source and destination.
analogy: Like a relay race. Each runner (router) carries the baton (packet) part of the way and hands it to the next runner closer to the finish line.
example: Your data might hop: your router → ISP router → regional hub → cross-country link → destination data center. Each hop is a router decision.
why_it_matters: Understanding routing explains why some connections are fast and others slow, and why the internet is resilient to failures.
checkpoint_question: If one route is blocked, can data still reach its destination?
expected_answer: Usually yes! The internet has multiple paths. Routers automatically find alternative routes. This redundancy makes the internet resilient to failures.
common_mistake: Thinking data takes the same path every time. Routes can change packet-by-packet based on network conditions.
code:
# See the route to a destination (terminal)
# Mac/Linux: traceroute google.com
# Windows: tracert google.com

# Shows each router hop:
# 1  192.168.1.1 (your router)
# 2  10.0.0.1 (ISP router)
# 3  ... (more hops)
# N  142.250.80.46 (destination)
key_insight: Your data typically goes through 10-20 routers to reach a website. Each router adds a small delay, which is part of latency.

title: Firewalls: Network Gatekeepers
explanation: A firewall filters network traffic based on rules. It can block unwanted connections and allow legitimate ones. Like a bouncer checking IDs - some connections are allowed in, others are turned away.
analogy: A firewall is like a security checkpoint. It checks each packet: 'Are you allowed through?' Based on rules, it lets traffic pass or blocks it.
example: Allow web traffic (ports 80, 443). Block unknown incoming connections. Allow outgoing traffic. These rules protect a network while letting it function.
why_it_matters: Firewalls are a basic security layer. Understanding them helps you troubleshoot connection issues and secure systems.
checkpoint_question: Why can you browse the web even with a firewall blocking incoming connections?
expected_answer: Firewalls typically allow outgoing requests and their responses. You initiate the web request (outgoing), and the firewall allows the response. It blocks unsolicited incoming connections.
common_mistake: Disabling firewalls to fix connection issues. Find the right rule instead - firewalls exist for protection.
key_insight: Firewalls can be hardware (network appliances) or software (running on your computer). Most operating systems have built-in software firewalls.

title: Latency vs Bandwidth
explanation: Bandwidth is how much data can flow per second (like pipe width). Latency is how long data takes to arrive (like pipe length). Fast download needs high bandwidth. Quick response needs low latency. Different problems.
analogy: Bandwidth = how many cars can fit on a highway. Latency = how long the highway is. A 100-lane highway doesn't help if it's 1000 miles long and you need quick delivery.
example: Streaming needs bandwidth (lots of data). Gaming needs low latency (quick response). A satellite link has high bandwidth but high latency (signal travels to space and back).
why_it_matters: Understanding this helps you diagnose network issues. 'Slow internet' could be bandwidth OR latency - different causes, different fixes.
checkpoint_question: Why do video calls freeze more on satellite internet than regular internet?
expected_answer: Satellite has high latency - signals travel to space and back (~600ms). Real-time conversation needs low latency. The bandwidth might be fine, but the delay makes conversation awkward.
common_mistake: Thinking faster internet speed (bandwidth) always fixes lag. Gaming lag is usually latency, which speed upgrades don't fix.
code:
# Check latency (ping)
# Terminal: ping google.com
# Output: time=15ms (that's the latency)

# Low latency: < 50ms (fast games/calls)
# Medium: 50-100ms (acceptable)
# High: > 100ms (noticeable lag)

# Bandwidth measured in Mbps (megabits per second)
# 100 Mbps = fast downloads
# Different from latency!
key_insight: Light in fiber can circle Earth in about 130ms. That's a physical limit - no technology can reduce latency below the speed of light.

title: Cookies: Remembering Users
explanation: Cookies are small data pieces websites store in your browser. They let websites remember you - keeping you logged in, saving preferences, tracking items in a cart. The browser sends cookies back with each request.
analogy: Like a wristband at a theme park. You get it once (login), then show it at every ride (request) so they know who you are without asking again.
example: You log into Amazon. It sets a cookie. Next request, browser sends cookie. Amazon knows you're still you. You stay logged in without entering password again.
why_it_matters: Cookies enable personalized web experiences. Understanding them helps you understand privacy concerns and how web apps maintain state.
checkpoint_question: Why does clearing cookies log you out of websites?
expected_answer: The cookie contained your login session identifier. Without it, the website doesn't know you're logged in. You're a new unknown visitor.
common_mistake: Thinking cookies are dangerous. Most are harmless (session cookies). Tracking cookies raise privacy concerns but aren't malware.
code:
# Cookie set by server (in HTTP response)
Set-Cookie: session=abc123; Secure; HttpOnly

# Browser sends cookie back (in HTTP request)
Cookie: session=abc123

# Server sees abc123 and knows who you are
key_insight: Third-party cookies (from other sites) are used for tracking across websites. Browsers are increasingly blocking them for privacy.

title: WebSockets: Two-Way Communication
explanation: HTTP is request-response: client asks, server answers. WebSockets keep a connection open for two-way messaging. Either side can send messages anytime. Essential for real-time apps like chat and live updates.
analogy: HTTP is like email (send, wait for reply). WebSockets are like a phone call (both can talk anytime, connection stays open).
example: Chat app: with HTTP, you'd poll 'any new messages?' constantly. With WebSockets, new messages are pushed instantly when they arrive.
why_it_matters: Modern real-time apps (chat, notifications, live sports, collaboration tools) depend on WebSockets.
checkpoint_question: Why not just use HTTP for a chat app?
expected_answer: HTTP requires the client to ask for updates. For instant messages, you'd constantly poll, wasting bandwidth and adding delay. WebSockets let the server push messages instantly.
common_mistake: Using WebSockets for everything. They're great for real-time but overkill for regular web pages. Use HTTP for request-response, WebSockets for real-time.
key_insight: WebSockets start as HTTP, then 'upgrade' to WebSocket protocol. That's why WebSocket URLs start with ws:// or wss:// (secure).

title: CDNs: Content Nearby
explanation: A CDN (Content Delivery Network) copies your content to servers worldwide. Users get content from a nearby server instead of one far away. This reduces latency and load on your main server.
analogy: Like having warehouses in every city vs one central warehouse. Customers get packages faster from the local warehouse.
example: Netflix doesn't stream from one server. Your video comes from a server in your city. Someone in Japan gets it from a server in Japan. Same content, served locally.
why_it_matters: CDNs make the web fast. Without them, users far from servers would have slow experiences. Most major sites use CDNs.
checkpoint_question: Why are CDNs especially helpful for images and videos?
expected_answer: Large files benefit most from proximity. A 10MB video from a server 100ms away takes much longer than from a server 10ms away. CDNs move heavy content closer to users.
common_mistake: Using CDNs for constantly-changing data. CDNs cache content - if it changes every second, caching doesn't help and might show stale data.
key_insight: Popular CDNs: Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront, Akamai, Fastly. They have servers in data centers worldwide.

title: Localhost: Your Own Computer
explanation: Localhost (127.0.0.1) is a special address meaning 'this computer'. When developing, you run a web server on localhost. Your browser connects to your own machine. No internet needed - it's all local.
analogy: Like talking to yourself. The message doesn't leave the room. Localhost means 'connect to myself.'
example: Run a development server on localhost:3000. Open browser to http://localhost:3000. Browser connects to your own computer's port 3000. No internet involved.
why_it_matters: Development happens on localhost. Understanding it helps you develop and test web applications without deploying to a real server.
checkpoint_question: Can someone else access your localhost server?
expected_answer: By default, no. Localhost means YOUR computer only. To let others access, you'd need to bind to your network IP or use tunneling tools like ngrok.
common_mistake: Thinking localhost needs internet. It's completely local - you can develop offline.
code:
# Common localhost ports during development:
# localhost:3000 - React, Node.js
# localhost:5000 - Flask (Python)
# localhost:8000 - Django (Python)
# localhost:8080 - Generic development

# These all mean 'connect to myself':
# localhost
# 127.0.0.1
# 0.0.0.0 (binds to all interfaces)
key_insight: 0.0.0.0 binds to all network interfaces, letting other devices connect. Useful for testing on your phone, but don't expose sensitive servers.

title: The OSI Model: Network Layers
explanation: Networks are organized in layers, each handling different concerns. Physical: cables and signals. Data Link: local network frames. Network: IP routing. Transport: TCP/UDP reliability. Application: HTTP, email, etc.
analogy: Like the postal system: writing (application), addressing (network), sorting facilities (transport), trucks and roads (physical). Each layer does its job without knowing details of others.
example: You send HTTP (application layer) over TCP (transport) using IP addressing (network) over WiFi (physical). Each layer wraps the previous.
why_it_matters: Understanding layers helps you troubleshoot: Is it a physical problem (cable)? Network problem (routing)? Application problem (your code)?
checkpoint_question: Why organize networks in layers?
expected_answer: Separation of concerns. You can change WiFi to Ethernet (physical) without changing your app code. Each layer can evolve independently. Different expertise for each layer.
common_mistake: Confusing layer problems. A bad cable (physical) looks like a network issue. Always check lower layers first.
key_insight: The OSI model has 7 layers. In practice, the TCP/IP model's 4 layers (application, transport, internet, link) is more commonly referenced.

title: Load Balancers: Distributing Traffic
explanation: A load balancer distributes incoming requests across multiple servers. Instead of one server handling everything, traffic spreads evenly. If one server fails, others continue serving. Essential for high availability.
analogy: Like a restaurant host directing diners to different tables so no single waiter is overwhelmed.
example: Million users hit your site. Load balancer sends requests to server 1, 2, 3, 4 in rotation. Each handles 250,000. Any server can fail without downtime.
why_it_matters: One server has limits. Load balancing enables scaling horizontally - add more servers for more capacity.
checkpoint_question: What happens to user sessions with load balancing?
expected_answer: Problem: user might hit different servers each request. Solutions: 'sticky sessions' (route same user to same server), or store sessions externally (Redis) so any server can access them.
common_mistake: Storing session data on individual servers. User hits different server, loses their session. Use shared session storage.
key_insight: Health checks: load balancer pings servers regularly. If one doesn't respond, it's removed from rotation until healthy again.

title: VPNs: Secure Tunnels
explanation: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) creates an encrypted tunnel between you and a server. All your traffic goes through this tunnel, encrypted and appearing to come from the VPN server's location. Protects privacy on untrusted networks.
analogy: Like a private underground tunnel to a trusted location. Traffic enters at your end, exits at the VPN server. Observers see the tunnel, not what's inside.
example: On coffee shop WiFi: without VPN, anyone could snoop. With VPN, traffic is encrypted to VPN server. The coffee shop sees encrypted gibberish.
why_it_matters: VPNs protect privacy on public WiFi and can bypass geographic restrictions. But they're not magic privacy shields.
checkpoint_question: Does a VPN make you anonymous?
expected_answer: No. The VPN server knows who you are and what you access. It hides your traffic from your ISP and local network, but moves trust to the VPN provider. They could log everything.
common_mistake: Thinking VPNs provide complete anonymity. They shift trust, not eliminate it. Your VPN provider sees your traffic.
key_insight: Corporate VPNs connect employees to company network securely from anywhere. Different use than privacy VPNs.

title: NAT: Sharing One Public IP
explanation: NAT (Network Address Translation) lets many devices share one public IP address. Your home router has one public IP, but many devices connect through it. NAT maps internal addresses to the single external address.
analogy: Like an office with one main phone number. Extensions internally, but the outside world sees one number. The receptionist routes calls.
example: Your phone, laptop, tablet all have internal IPs (192.168.x.x). The router has one public IP. NAT translates between them, routing responses to the right device.
why_it_matters: NAT is why we haven't run out of IPv4 addresses yet. Millions of devices hide behind shared IPs.
checkpoint_question: Why can't someone from the internet connect directly to your laptop?
expected_answer: Your laptop has a private IP behind NAT. The outside world only sees your router's public IP. Incoming connections go to the router, which doesn't know where to forward them unless you set up port forwarding.
common_mistake: Assuming your device has a public IP. Most home devices are behind NAT. Use port forwarding to expose services.
code:
# Private IP ranges (used behind NAT):
# 10.0.0.0 - 10.255.255.255
# 172.16.0.0 - 172.31.255.255
# 192.168.0.0 - 192.168.255.255

# Check your private IP: ifconfig / ipconfig
# Check public IP: curl ifconfig.me

# They'll be different - NAT maps between them
key_insight: NAT breaks the end-to-end principle: devices can't easily connect directly. This complicates peer-to-peer apps and gaming.

title: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3: Faster Web
explanation: HTTP/1.1 sends requests one at a time per connection. HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection. HTTP/3 uses UDP instead of TCP for even lower latency. Each version makes the web faster.
analogy: HTTP/1.1: one lane road. HTTP/2: multiple lanes on one road. HTTP/3: flying instead of driving - different approach entirely.
example: Web page needs 50 files. HTTP/1.1: request, wait, request, wait... HTTP/2: request all 50 together, receive as they're ready. Much faster.
why_it_matters: Modern websites have many resources. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 load them faster, improving user experience significantly.
checkpoint_question: Why does HTTP/3 use UDP instead of TCP?
expected_answer: TCP's reliability features add latency (handshakes, retransmissions). HTTP/3 builds reliability on top of UDP, customized for web needs. Faster connection setup and recovery from packet loss.
common_mistake: Manually enabling HTTP/2. It's usually automatic - browsers and servers negotiate the best protocol.
key_insight: Server push in HTTP/2: server sends resources before browser asks, if it knows they'll be needed. Proactive, not reactive.

title: GraphQL: Flexible Queries
explanation: GraphQL lets clients request exactly the data they need in a single query. Unlike REST (fixed endpoints, server decides what to return), GraphQL clients specify the shape of the response. Reduces over-fetching and under-fetching.
analogy: REST: ordering combo meals. GraphQL: ordering from a menu where you pick exactly each item. Get what you want, nothing more.
example: Mobile needs user name and avatar. Desktop needs full profile. One GraphQL endpoint, each asks for what they need. No multiple requests or wasted data.
why_it_matters: GraphQL is increasingly popular for APIs. It solves real problems with REST, especially for clients with varying data needs.
checkpoint_question: What problem does GraphQL solve that REST doesn't?
expected_answer: Over-fetching: REST returns fixed shapes, often more than needed. Under-fetching: need multiple requests to get related data. GraphQL: one request, exact data needed.
common_mistake: Using GraphQL for simple CRUD. REST is simpler when endpoints map cleanly to resources. GraphQL shines with complex, varied data needs.
key_insight: GraphQL has a schema defining what's queryable. Strong typing catches errors. Introspection lets tools auto-generate docs.

title: Microservices Communication
explanation: Microservices communicate via network, not function calls. Synchronous (HTTP/gRPC: wait for response) or asynchronous (message queues: fire and forget). Each has tradeoffs in latency, coupling, and complexity.
analogy: Synchronous: phone call (wait for answer). Asynchronous: text message (send and continue, read response later).
example: Order service needs user info. Sync: call user service, wait. Async: put message on queue, user service processes later, sends event when done.
why_it_matters: Communication patterns affect reliability, latency, and coupling. Choose patterns that match your requirements.
checkpoint_question: When would you choose asynchronous over synchronous communication?
expected_answer: When you don't need immediate response. When operations take long. When you want loose coupling. When you need to handle spikes (queue buffers). When eventual consistency is OK.
common_mistake: Making everything synchronous. Creates tight coupling, cascading failures, and latency accumulation. Use async where possible.
code:
# Synchronous: wait for response
user = http.get('/users/123')  # Blocks
process_order(user)

# Asynchronous: message queue
queue.publish('order_created', {'user_id': 123, 'items': [...]})
# Continue without waiting

# Another service handles it later
@queue.subscribe('order_created')
def handle_order(message):
    user = get_user(message['user_id'])
    send_confirmation(user, message)
key_insight: Event-driven architecture: services publish events, interested services subscribe. Loose coupling - producers don't know consumers.

title: Common Network Debugging Tools
explanation: ping: check if host is reachable. traceroute: see the path packets take. curl: make HTTP requests. netstat/ss: see open connections. nslookup/dig: DNS queries. tcpdump/Wireshark: inspect packet contents.
analogy: Like a doctor's toolkit. Different tools diagnose different problems. Know which to use when.
example: Site unreachable: ping (is it up?), then traceroute (where does it fail?), then curl (what does HTTP say?). Narrow down the problem layer.
why_it_matters: Network issues happen constantly. Knowing diagnostic tools helps you quickly find whether it's DNS, routing, firewall, or application.
checkpoint_question: A website doesn't load. How would you diagnose it?
expected_answer: 1) ping: is the server reachable? 2) nslookup: is DNS resolving? 3) curl: what HTTP response? 4) Check firewall. Narrow down which layer is failing.
common_mistake: Assuming it's the server when it's DNS. Or assuming it's the network when it's the application. Test each layer systematically.
code:
# Check if host is reachable
ping google.com

# See the route packets take
traceroute google.com

# DNS lookup
nslookup google.com
dig google.com

# Make HTTP request
curl -v https://google.com

# See open connections
netstat -an | grep LISTEN
ss -tuln

# Inspect packets (requires sudo)
tcpdump -i any port 80
key_insight: Start simple. ping before tcpdump. Most problems are obvious once you check the right thing.

title: HTTP Status Codes: What They Mean
explanation: Every HTTP response has a status code. 2xx = success. 3xx = redirect. 4xx = client error (you messed up). 5xx = server error (they messed up). The code tells you what happened without reading the response body.
analogy: Like a traffic light. Green (200) = go ahead. Yellow (301) = take a different route. Red (404/500) = stop, something's wrong.
example: 200 OK (success), 201 Created (new resource made), 301 Moved (use new URL), 404 Not Found (bad URL), 500 Server Error (server crashed).
why_it_matters: Status codes help you debug quickly. 404 means wrong URL. 500 means check server logs. 401 means auth problem. Know the common ones.
checkpoint_question: User gets 403 Forbidden. What's wrong?
expected_answer: They're authenticated (not 401) but not authorized for this resource. They don't have permission. Check their role/permissions, not their login.
common_mistake: Using 200 OK for errors with error message in body. Use proper status codes - clients and tools depend on them for handling.
code:
# Common status codes to know:
# 200 OK - Request succeeded
# 201 Created - New resource created
# 204 No Content - Success, nothing to return
# 301 Moved Permanently - Use new URL
# 304 Not Modified - Use cached version
# 400 Bad Request - Invalid request format
# 401 Unauthorized - Need to log in
# 403 Forbidden - Logged in but no permission
# 404 Not Found - Resource doesn't exist
# 429 Too Many Requests - Rate limited
# 500 Internal Server Error - Server crashed
# 502 Bad Gateway - Upstream server failed
# 503 Service Unavailable - Server overloaded
key_insight: 401 = who are you? (authentication). 403 = I know who you are, but you can't do this (authorization). Different problems, different fixes.

title: CORS: Why Your API Call Failed
explanation: Browsers block requests from one website to another domain (security). CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is how servers say 'requests from this domain are OK'. Without it, your frontend can't call your API if they're on different domains.
analogy: Like a bouncer with a guest list. Your website (guest) tries to access another domain (club). The server checks if you're on the allowed list.
example: Frontend on mysite.com, API on api.mysite.com. Browser blocks the request. Add CORS header 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: mysite.com' to API. Now it works.
why_it_matters: CORS errors are common and confusing. Understanding CORS helps you fix them and avoid overly permissive settings that create security holes.
checkpoint_question: Why does the browser enforce CORS, not the server?
expected_answer: To protect users. Without CORS, malicious websites could make requests to your bank using your cookies. Browsers prevent this. Servers just indicate what's allowed.
common_mistake: Setting Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * in production. Allows any website to call your API. Be specific about which origins are allowed.
code:
# Browser error:
# Access to fetch at 'api.example.com' from origin
# 'mysite.com' has been blocked by CORS policy

# Server fix (Python/Flask):
from flask import Flask
from flask_cors import CORS

app = Flask(__name__)
CORS(app, origins=['https://mysite.com'])

# Or manually set headers:
@app.after_request
def add_cors(response):
    response.headers['Access-Control-Allow-Origin'] = 'https://mysite.com'
    return response
key_insight: CORS preflight: for complex requests, browser first sends OPTIONS request to check if the real request is allowed. Server must handle OPTIONS.

title: WebSockets: Two-Way Real-Time Connection
explanation: HTTP is request-response: client asks, server answers. WebSockets create a persistent two-way connection. Either side can send messages anytime. Ideal for chat, live updates, games.
analogy: HTTP is like texting - you send, wait for reply. WebSocket is like a phone call - both can talk anytime, connection stays open.
example: Chat app: establish WebSocket once. User sends message, server receives instantly. Server broadcasts to others, they receive instantly. No polling needed.
why_it_matters: WebSockets enable real-time features that would be inefficient with HTTP polling. Lower latency, less overhead, true push from server.
checkpoint_question: When would you use HTTP instead of WebSockets?
expected_answer: For regular request/response (forms, page loads, APIs). WebSockets have connection overhead. If you don't need real-time push, HTTP is simpler and scales better.
common_mistake: Using WebSockets for everything. They're harder to scale (persistent connections), harder to load balance, and don't cache. Use for real-time needs only.
key_insight: WebSocket starts as HTTP upgrade request. After handshake, protocol switches. Same port (80/443), firewall-friendly.

title: CDNs: Serving Content Close to Users
explanation: A CDN (Content Delivery Network) caches your content on servers worldwide. Users download from nearest server instead of your origin. Faster load times, less load on your servers, better for global users.
analogy: Like having warehouses in every city instead of shipping everything from one factory. Closer warehouse = faster delivery.
example: User in Tokyo requests image. Without CDN: request goes to server in New York, 200ms. With CDN: request goes to Tokyo edge server, 20ms.
why_it_matters: CDNs make websites fast globally. They also protect against traffic spikes and DDoS attacks by distributing load.
checkpoint_question: What content should go on a CDN?
expected_answer: Static content: images, CSS, JavaScript, videos, fonts. Content that's the same for all users. Dynamic content (personalized) usually shouldn't be cached on CDN.
common_mistake: Caching private content on CDN. If CDN caches user-specific data, wrong users might see it. Set proper Cache-Control headers for dynamic content.
code:
# Cache-Control headers tell CDN what to cache

# Cache for 1 year (static assets with hash in filename)
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# Cache for 1 hour, revalidate after
Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600, must-revalidate

# Never cache (private/dynamic content)
Cache-Control: private, no-store

# CDN providers:
# - Cloudflare (free tier)
# - AWS CloudFront
# - Fastly
# - Akamai
key_insight: CDNs cache based on URL. Change URL (add version hash) to bust cache. styles.css?v=2 or styles.abc123.css.
